Midterm elections generally are dangerous territory for the political party that holds the White House and/or Congress. For 2026 that means ​that President Donald Trump and his Republicans controlling the US Senate and House of Representatives are in perilous political positions.

The midterms can be an opportunity for voters to, in effect, grade the president's performance, and possibly trigger White House course corrections if they receive ​low marks. On 3 November, voters will decide control of the US Congress, 36 governorships and thousands of state and local offices, with millions of ballots already cast in early voting by mail or in person. [...] These are the midterm elections, held halfway through a president’s four-year term. The presidency itself is not on the ballot, but the results will decide who controls Congress and many state capitals for the rest of President Donald Trump’s term. In 20 of the last 22 midterm elections, the president’s party has lost ground.

So, what can we expect from this year's vote?

results.content: The Constitution establishes that Congress, not the executive branch, has significant authority over congressional elections, so most efforts to regulate voting rights have focused on congressional elections as places of intervention. The constitution is resiliently federalist in terms of delegating large chunks of authority to states and localities, and in this case it reminds us of why that can be a bulwark of defense against tyranny.
